context_brief: Independent first view of PROMPT.md, written before seeing Claude Code's Phase 1 report, so my review later is not anchored to its conclusions.
findings_or_changes: RISK 1 — You are the bus, and buses drop packets. There is no direct Muse-to-Claude-Code channel; every handoff is manual copy-paste by a human. The state machine (READY/BLOCKED/DONE, hashes, evidence IDs) is only as reliable as relay discipline. The most likely failure of this whole system is not a bad framework choice — it is a stale or lossy handoff between chats. Mitigation exists in the prompt (canonical records, Section 4 envelopes) but nothing enforces it except your habits.

RISK 2 — Phase 1 scope vs. the monetization goal. The prompt asks for a framework comparison PLUS a skills/MCP/security-tool audit PLUS a threat model PLUS four Mermaid diagrams PLUS a routing matrix before any revenue signal exists. That is days of research cost. With your free weekly allowance already at 100% (see P1-MUSE-01), every hour of Phase 1 burns the additional-token balance. Phase 1 needs a hard timebox or it becomes the project.

RISK 3 — The Ollama leg is a phantom tier on your current hardware. The prompt correctly says 'inspect actual machine capacity,' but the whole routing design (T1 local tier for 'high-volume' work) assumes local models that an M1/8GB Mac cannot meaningfully run. If the capacity check is honest, the answer is 'no local tier until the 3090 build exists' — and the routing matrix must be designed for two environments, not three, until then.

RISK 4 — Security by convention, not by mechanism. Approval gates and 'never do X' rules depend on model obedience; Section 7 admits 'a security skill is not itself a security boundary,' yet the design still leans on LLM judgment plus your manual approvals. Copy-paste handoffs are also a secret-leak vector (a pasted log or file can carry a key). The threat model should treat the human relay as part of the attack surface.

RISK 5 — Provenance will decay before Phase 2 automation exists. Hashes, evidence IDs, freshness dates and the status board are manual until the backbone is built — a chicken-and-egg problem: the system that enforces rigor does not exist during the phase that needs it most. Related business risk: this is a regulated food product; supplier quotes and MOQs cannot be obtained without contact (approval-gated), so the timeline to first revenue is months, not weeks. Treat Phase 4's go/no-go as the real monetization gate and do not let sunk Phase 1-3 cost bias it.

MUSE SHOULD OWN: web research synthesis with citations and source ledgers; independent challenger/red-team review of Claude Code's reports; research planning, decision framing and option matrices; plain-language explanations and tutoring; structured handoff packets. These match verified capabilities (live web, writing, synthesis, critique).

MUSE SHOULD NOT OWN: running code or tests, or verifying anything executed (my VM is not your Mac and not your repo); holding the source of truth (your repo is canonical — my files are drafts until you file them); contacting anyone or taking external actions; definitive regulatory or legal interpretation; usage metering on your side; or serving as the system of record for state.
Q1: Confirm the market jurisdiction — is the Greater Toronto Area / Ontario / Canada the launch market? This drives the entire regulatory workstream (Health Canada/CFIA vs. other regimes).
Q2: What is the Phase 1 budget — how much time and token spend may the research burn before the approval gate? (Your free weekly allowance is already at 100%; see P1-MUSE-01.)
Q3: Is 'Dot' a real separate tool you have, or am I playing the Dot/Muse role? This changes what handoff formats and capabilities to assume.
Q4: Ollama now or later — should Claude Code benchmark local capacity in Phase 1, or do we formally defer the local tier until the 3090 PC exists?
Q5: Where does the canonical repo live (your Mac, Claude Code's machine?) and how do I get read access to it — you paste/upload files, or something else?
